starters.name: Monolith
starters.summary: A clinic's booking site, staff screens and API in one Django app, deployed as one unit behind NGINX
useWhen: A new product or a small team, where one deployable keeps change cheap.
Explaining where a request goes before any of it is split out.
Scaling by running more identical copies behind a load balancer.
watchOutFor: Every change ships the whole application, and one bad release takes everything down.
Slow calls inside a request, like sending a text, slow every user; move them to a job.
Module lines inside the codebase blur unless they are kept on purpose.

starters.name: Modular Monolith
starters.summary: A course platform as one Spring Boot deployable with Catalog, Enrollment, Billing and Notifications modules
useWhen: You want clear ownership without the cost of distributed services.
Preparing a monolith to split later, one module at a time.
Several teams share one codebase and need lines they cannot cross by accident.
watchOutFor: Module boundaries only hold if calls go through the public interface; enforce it in a build test.
A shared database server makes it easy to join another module's tables; grant each module its own schema.
In-process events vanish on a crash unless they are stored before they are handled.

starters.name: Microservices
starters.summary: A food-delivery platform: services behind Kong, each owning its data, talking by gRPC and Kafka events
useWhen: Teams need to deploy and scale parts of the system independently.
Mapping which service owns which data, and how the others reach it.
Deciding which calls must be synchronous and which can be events.
watchOutFor: Calls between services fail and are slow in ways in-process calls are not; guard them.
Every synchronous call chains availability: one service down can stop the main path.
Queries that span services need their own design: a read model, an API composer or a BFF.

starters.name: Event-Driven
starters.summary: One event, many reactions: a topic fans out to a queue per subscriber, with a dead-letter queue for failures
useWhen: Several consumers react to the same change without the producer knowing them.
One slow or failing consumer must not hold up the others.
Showing retries, idempotent consumers and where failed messages go.
watchOutFor: Delivery is at least once: every consumer must handle duplicates.
Events can arrive out of order across queues; don't let consumers assume an order.
One request is harder to follow end to end; keep event ids in your logs and traces.
An event's shape is a contract with consumers you may not know about. Version it.

starters.name: Hexagonal
starters.summary: A bank's transfers core owns its ports; REST, a job, JPA, Kafka and a fraud vendor plug in as adapters
useWhen: Keeping business rules independent of frameworks, databases and vendors.
Testing the core with in-memory adapters, without infrastructure.
The same use case is driven from several places: HTTP, a job, a message.
watchOutFor: More indirection than a small service may need.
Ports drift into thin wrappers if they mirror one adapter or one vendor's API.
Arrows here read at runtime (port, then the adapter behind it); source dependencies point the other way, inward.

starters.name: Backend for Frontend
starters.summary: Web, mobile and TV each get a backend shaped for their screens, over shared platform APIs
useWhen: Web, mobile and TV need different shapes and sizes of the same data.
Frontend teams want to change their API without coordinating every release.
A screen should load in one round trip instead of many calls from a slow network.
watchOutFor: Business rules creeping into BFFs and drifting apart; keep them in the platform APIs.
One more service per client to build, run and keep secure.
A BFF that waits on every call is as slow as its slowest one; set budgets and degrade.

starters.name: CQRS
starters.summary: A bank's payments write events on one side; projections build balances and searchable history on the other
useWhen: Reads and writes have very different shapes or loads.
Several read models (a balance, a search index) answer from one source of truth.
Explaining eventual consistency between the two sides.
watchOutFor: Reads lag behind writes; the UI must cope with its own change not showing yet.
Two models to keep in step as the domain changes, and projections to rebuild.
An event a projection can't apply leaves that read model stale until someone acts.

starters.name: Medallion
starters.summary: A ride-hailing lakehouse refines raw trips into Bronze, Silver and Gold, and quarantines bad rows
useWhen: Building analytics on data from several operational sources at different cadences.
Showing where data quality is enforced, and where rows that fail it go.
You need to rebuild cleaned data after a bug fix without asking the sources again.
watchOutFor: Each layer stores another copy of the data, and each copy costs storage and compute.
Late or corrected source data has to be reprocessed through every layer after it.
A quarantine table nobody triages quietly drops data from every report.

starters.name: Kappa
starters.summary: Card fraud scoring from one durable log: live scoring, and a full replay to rebuild with new rules
useWhen: Real-time views where reprocessing history must use the same code as live processing.
Replacing a separate batch layer with one stream processor and a log you can replay.
Changing scoring rules and rebuilding a view side by side before switching to it.
watchOutFor: Replaying a long log takes hours and cluster capacity; plan the cutover.
The log's retention decides how far back you can rebuild.
Logic that reads the clock instead of event time scores a replay differently from live.

starters.name: Change Data Capture
starters.summary: A marketplace streams committed listing changes from PostgreSQL to search, cache and warehouse
useWhen: Keeping search, caches or analytics in sync with a database without dual writes.
Feeding several derived views, each at its own pace, from one source of truth.
Backfilling a new view from a snapshot without querying production.
watchOutFor: Derived views are eventually consistent: they can show the old value for a moment.
Events mirror the table: a renamed column breaks every consumer.
If the connector stops for longer than the WAL is kept, it must snapshot again.

starters.name: Saga – Orchestration
starters.summary: One orchestrator books a trip step by step, and cancels the done steps in reverse when the card is declined
useWhen: A workflow spans several services and must undo completed steps on failure.
You want one place that knows the workflow's state and can answer "where is my booking?".
Steps have a fixed order and the riskiest one can go last.
watchOutFor: The orchestrator can grow into a god service that owns other teams' business rules.
Every step needs a compensation that really undoes it, and is idempotent when retried.
A compensation is a new transaction, not a rollback: the seat was held for a while.
Without durable workflow state, a crash mid-saga leaves steps nobody will undo.

starters.name: Saga – Choreography
starters.summary: A food order moves through payment and kitchen by events alone, and unwinds by events when a restaurant says no
useWhen: Few steps, owned by different teams, that already communicate through events.
Avoiding a central workflow service that every change has to go through.
Each step can decide on its own what to do when it sees a fact.
watchOutFor: The whole workflow is visible only by following the events; trace a correlation id.
Nothing times out a stuck saga unless some service is made responsible for it.
Cyclic dependencies between services creep in as steps grow.
Compensations are reactions too: a missed event leaves money taken for a cancelled order.

starters.name: Transactional Outbox
starters.summary: A bank transfer and its event commit in one transaction; Debezium publishes it after, and consumers drop duplicates
useWhen: A state change and its event must never disagree.
Publishing events from a service that owns a relational database.
The broker must not be on the request path: a Kafka outage should not block writes.
watchOutFor: Events arrive at least once and slightly late; every consumer must deduplicate.
The outbox table grows unless rows are deleted once published.
Ordering holds only per message key; choose the key for the order consumers need.
The relay is one more thing to run and monitor: lag means late events.

starters.name: Video streaming platform
starters.summary: A whole streaming service: devices, edge, playback, discovery, data and an ISP-hosted video edge
useWhen: Seeing every Draft Canvas feature at work in one realistic system before drawing your own.
Explaining how video reaches screens: playback decisions in the cloud, bytes from the edge.
Starting a system-design discussion about a large consumer platform.
watchOutFor: It is a big picture on purpose: present it flow by flow rather than all at once.
Scale numbers are illustrative; replace them with your own before you reason from them.
Three connectors are portals and the file is format 29, so it needs a current Draft Canvas.

starters.name: Music streaming service
starters.summary: A whole music service: playback from a CDN, an AI DJ, weekly mixes, royalties and artist releases
useWhen: Seeing how an AI agent, batch jobs and a live API share one realistic system.
Explaining how one play becomes a song, a recommendation and a royalty payment.
Starting a system-design discussion about a consumer platform with a data business.
watchOutFor: It is a big picture on purpose: present it flow by flow rather than all at once.
Scale numbers are illustrative; replace them with your own before you reason from them.
Two connectors are portals and the file is format 29, so it needs a current Draft Canvas.

starters.name: Order processing
starters.summary: A shop takes the payment, queues fulfilment, and parks orders the warehouse keeps refusing
useWhen: Learning how shapes, connectors, flows, notes and drill-down views read on the canvas.
A request must answer fast while slower work, like booking a shipment, happens after.
Sketching any queue-and-worker design with a failure path.
watchOutFor: Storing the order and sending the command are two writes; pair it with the Transactional Outbox.
Competing consumers process orders out of order; nothing here may depend on it.
A dead-letter queue nobody watches is just a slower way to lose orders.
